title: In-house super fund teams cost more and return less, study finds
full_text:
Superannuation funds that have brought their investment teams in-house have performed worse over the past three years than their peers that rely on outsourced managers, and have cost their members more in fees, says one of the country's top equities research houses.
MST Marquee analyst Lafitani Sotiriou says "the prevailing myth that scale and internalisation is helping industry funds is not proven", in a wide-ranging note on the $4.7 trillion retirement savings sector that examines their investment returns, expenses and growing market influence.
Two of the nation's biggest funds, AustralianSuper and Aware Super, had increased their internally managed funds from about 25 per cent to 37 per cent in the past five years, said Sotiriou.
Their returns above benchmarks had halved in that same period and started to lag major rivals using external managers, his analysis found.
"Hostplus, the only fund in the top five largest industry funds we discussed earlier that has not moved to internalise ... [remains] a clear case study of external management being a successful recipe," he said.
Compared with several funds - including UniSuper, CareSuper and Prime Super - Sotiriou said Hostplus' return of 8.32 per cent in its balanced fund over the past decade "was the highest of any of the six funds we assess". The analyst said internalised funds also were paying higher investment costs per dollar under management, while "the externally managed funds have seen reduced investment cost ratios".
"In the three years since material internalisation has occurred, our pool of funds shows evidence that internalised funds are underperforming externally managed funds, while also seeing outsized cost growth," he said.
Sotiriou's research challenges the narrative of some of the country's largest superannuation funds, including the $410 billion AustralianSuper, that internalised investments deliver better outcomes for investors than the once-dominant outsourced model.
It also follows a warning from one of the country's most respected investors, David Paradice, that the growing rate of internalised investment expertise at super funds risks further closures of active money managers. Only a quarter of active Australian large-capitalisation equity managers outperformed the S&P/ASX 200 Index in the year to June 30, the weakest result in seven years, according to Morningstar.
That accelerated an exodus from local funds, with investors such as big superannuation funds pulling $6.6 billion in mandates last financial year and almost $22 billion in five years.
At the same time, funds tracking Australian indices attracted a record $15.5 billion last year and $40.2 billion over five years.
The underperformance and mandate withdrawals have also led to the shutdown of institutional equities funds, including Platypus Asset Management's and Tyndall Asset Management's large-capitalisation strategies.
More recently, Cooper Investors has flagged a significant downsizing. Peter Cooper's eponymous firm has gone from managing about $14 billion to less than $2 billion in three years.
Paradice blamed the annual superannuation performance test, introduced by the Morrison government in 2021, which he said had distorted equity markets as big super funds kept buying the largest stocks irrespective of valuation, wrong-footing active managers investing in core fundamentals.
Sotiriou also criticised the performance test, arguing that it "inherently favours passive investing" and led to the super sector becoming a "passive free rider".
Rainmaker, a market research firm, said the average proportion of internally managed assets across 40 super funds had jumped from 9.3 per cent in 2019 to 22.1 per cent last year. It said the largest increase was among Australian equities and cash holdings. Private equity holdings were increasingly being managed externally.
AustralianSuper began shifting the management of infrastructure assets from in-house to external managers last year after underperforming the broader market. It declined to comment on the MST research.
"The research shows internalisation is a defining feature of Australia's superannuation sector, although the trend is far from uniform across all asset classes," said Rainmaker associate director of research Camille Schmidt.
"While the trend towards in-house asset management is expected to continue, the emerging model is selective internalisation across both public and private markets, combined with external managers where they provide differentiated expertise, access, capacity or risk diversification," she said.
MST's Sotiriou said industry super fund allocations to private equity were nearly four times higher than retail funds. While these assets provided diversification and stable returns, he cautioned that "government pressure to contribute to nation building" increased the risk of misallocation.
There were also risks around valuation methodologies, and illiquidity in some private equity investments was becoming a concern as some funds moved towards net outflows as the population aged, he added.
Sotiriou said persistent cost overruns with local infrastructure projects could ultimately create a material drag on returns for members.
"Deloitte estimates that of the 13 publicly funded projects valued at $10 billion in February 2026, the latest cost estimates had blown out by $130 billion."
